title: Indian Food Grows Up: No Longer 'Modern', Now the Food of Modern India
excerpt: Condé Nast Traveller India's verdict marks a turning point: after the molecular-gimmick era, the country's best kitchens are cooking with regional confidence — and diaspora restaurants are following.
body:
• Condé Nast Traveller India's verdict on the country's dining scene: the movement has outgrown the "modern Indian" label — "it is no longer modern Indian food; it is the food of modern India."
  • The first wave — Indian Accent's Manish Mehrotra, Gaggan Anand's modernist tasting menus — proved Indian flavors could sit at the global table; the backlash against gimmicks (sambar foams, deconstructed everything) forced the cuisine to grow up.
  • Today's leading kitchens dig into regional roots instead: Thomas Zacharias's sol kadi ceviche at The Bombay Canteen, heritage recipes from home kitchens, and writers like Sonal Ved documenting hyper-local cuisines state by state.
  • What to order: at a good Indian restaurant now, ask what region the menu draws from — look for dishes named for their origins (Konkani, Chettinad, Kashmiri, Goan) rather than generic "curry" labels; that's where the confident new cooking lives.

Somewhere along the way, Indian food stopped asking for permission. That is the argument Condé Nast Traveller India makes in its latest survey of the country's dining scene, distilled into a single line: "It is no longer modern Indian food; it is the food of modern India." The distinction sounds subtle. It isn't.

"It is no longer modern Indian food; it is the food of modern India."

— Condé Nast Traveller India

"Modern Indian" was always a borrowed frame — Western techniques applied to Indian flavors, plated for diners who needed the cuisine translated. "The food of modern India" claims something else: a cuisine confident enough to be itself, on its own terms.

The first wave proved a point, then overstayed

The modern-Indian movement began as a liberation. As food writer Vir Sanghvi has noted, chefs like Manish Mehrotra at Indian Accent and Gaggan Anand in Bangkok took Indian flavors and said they could be put into other things — tasting menus, global formats, techniques borrowed from anywhere. For a cuisine long trapped between five-star butter chicken and the neighborhood tandoori joint, it was a genuine breakthrough.

Then came the imitators. Forbes India's examination of the trend documented the moment it curdled: upstart restaurants with no grasp of flavor profiles serving Maggi in makhni sauce and coriander foam that couldn't be tasted. To diners, "modern Indian" began to mean gimmicks without substance — a deconstructed vada pav with neither the style nor the substance of the original.

The turn inward

What replaced the gimmick era was not a retreat but a deepening. The chefs who endured dug into India's own culinary traditions rather than outward at global trends. Thomas Zacharias at Mumbai's The Bombay Canteen built dishes like a sol kadi ceviche — a tribute to the Konkani drink, not a copy of a Peruvian one. Menus began to read like maps: Chettinad, Kashmiri, Goan, Konkani.

The same turn is happening on the page. Journalist and cookbook author Sonal Ved's "Whose Samosa Is It Anyway?" argues there was never one Indian cuisine to modernize in the first place — only hyper-local traditions, from Indus Valley roots to post-liberalization plates, each with its own narrative. You can't deconstruct what you haven't understood, and the new generation of cooks seems to have taken that to heart.

What it means for diaspora diners

This shift travels well. In New York, chef Chintan Pandya built his reputation at Rahi and Adda on food he calls "unapologetically Indian" — refusing to serve British inventions like tikka masala or tone down spices for local palates, and earning serious critical acclaim for it. The diaspora diner no longer has to choose between the curryhouse greatest-hits menu and a tasting menu that treats Indian food as raw material for someone else's technique.

The practical upshot is a better question to ask at the table. Instead of "is this authentic," try "where is this from." The confident new Indian cooking — in Mumbai, in London, in New Jersey — answers with a region, a community, sometimes a grandmother. That is what the food of modern India sounds like.
